name: Third-Party and Vendor Model Risk
question: What happens to us when our model provider changes, leaks or goes down?
summary: When a bank or broker runs its agent on someone else’s model, the provider’s terms, versions and outages become the firm’s own risk, and regulators still hold the firm accountable. Vendor model risk management covers due diligence before signing (training use, retention and zero data retention, data residency, SOC 2, ISO/IEC 27001 and 42001), contracts with SLAs, audit rights and incident notice, pinned model versions with evals on every change, concentration risk with a tested fallback and an exit plan, and ongoing monitoring. The regulatory duties themselves sit in the DPDP and RBI and SEBI techniques; this one is the vendor-facing engineering and contracting that meets them.
useCases: Before signing with an LLM provider or AI vendor
Any regulated workload that runs on a third-party model
When a provider announces a deprecation or changes its terms

steps.title: Due diligence before data flows
steps.text: Godavari Bank, a fictional private bank, checks four things before any complaint text reaches the provider: no training on its data, retention it has agreed (zero data retention here, instead of the default 30 days of logs), processing in India, and current SOC 2 Type II and ISO/IEC 27001 reports whose scope covers the API it will use.

steps.title: A contract you can enforce
steps.text: The contract turns assurances into obligations: a 99.9% availability SLA, notice of incidents within 6 hours so the bank can meet its own CERT-In and DPDP clocks, audit and access rights for the bank and its regulator, notice before new sub-processors, and an exit clause for data return and deletion.

steps.title: Pin a dated version
steps.text: The code names a dated snapshot, not a floating alias. With an alias the provider can change the model behind the same name, and the bank’s complaint summaries change with no release on its side.

steps.title: Evals on every change
steps.text: A deprecation notice or a new snapshot triggers the eval suite: 400 labelled complaints. If the score drops more than 2 points below the baseline, the change is blocked and the pin stays. Otherwise the new version is proposed through the normal release review.

steps.title: A tested fallback
steps.text: All calls go through one function. If the primary provider is down or times out, the same request goes to a second provider on its own pinned version, with the same data terms. A fallback counts only if it has carried real traffic in a drill.

steps.title: Keep watching, and plan the exit
steps.text: Each month someone checks deprecation notices, terms changes, SLA reports and certificate expiry, and drills the failover. Once a year the exit plan is rehearsed: which prompts move, which evals prove the new model, how data comes back and is deleted, and how long it takes.

pros: Customer data terms are known and enforceable, not assumed
Provider changes arrive as reviewed releases, not surprises
A provider outage becomes a short failover instead of a day offline
Answers the vendor questions RBI, SEBI and DPDP reviews will ask
cons: Zero data retention and enterprise terms can need a larger commitment
Pinned versions still retire, so migrations and evals recur
A second provider means porting prompts and re-running evals twice
Contract negotiation and yearly reviews take legal and risk time
avoidWhen: A throwaway prototype on synthetic data, with no customer data and no production users
Fully self-hosted open-weight models, where the risk moves to your own operations rather than a vendor (still pin and eval)

practice.scenario: Godavari Bank, a fictional private bank, summarises 2,00,000 customer complaint conversations a month with an overseas LLM provider, on default terms and a floating model alias. One Tuesday the complaint summaries start dropping the amount in dispute: the provider had moved the alias to a new snapshot. Two months later the provider has an 8-hour incident and the assistant is down all day. The fix was a vendor programme, not a better prompt: zero data retention agreed in writing, an India region, a pinned snapshot with a 400-case eval run before any change, a second provider behind one gateway that is drilled monthly, and a written exit plan. Inspection findings went from 4 to 0.

industries.use: Complaint summarisation and reply drafting on a provider’s model, reviewed under RBI outsourcing expectations
Research summaries and client chat on a vendor model, where SEBI Regulation 16C keeps the broker responsible for the output
Clinical note drafting on a hosted model, where retention, region and, in the US, HIPAA business associate terms decide what may be sent

practice.analogy: Renting a delivery van instead of owning one. You read the rental terms, insist the company does not swap the engine without telling you, keep a second rental firm’s number on file, and know how you would move to your own van. The parcels are still yours if they arrive late.

library.name: LiteLLM
library.what: An open-source gateway and Python SDK with one interface over many model providers; its Router takes pinned model names, retries and fallbacks between deployments.

practice.note: Model names are examples of dated snapshots; use the snapshot names your providers currently list, and check their deprecation pages. run_eval_suite and alert_risk_team are stubs for your own eval harness and alerting. Provider keys are read from environment variables. Data terms such as zero data retention are agreed with the provider, not set in this code. Educational, not legal advice.

samples.code:
from litellm import Router

PRIMARY = "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929"     # dated snapshot, not an alias
FALLBACK = "openai/gpt-4.1-2025-04-14"               # second provider, same data terms

router = Router(
    model_list=[
        {"model_name": "complaints", "litellm_params": {"model": PRIMARY, "timeout": 20}},
        {"model_name": "complaints-backup", "litellm_params": {"model": FALLBACK, "timeout": 20}},
    ],
    fallbacks=[{"complaints": ["complaints-backup"]}],
    num_retries=1,
)

VENDOR_CHECKS = {
    "trains_on_our_data": False,
    "retention_days": 0,                 # zero data retention agreed in the contract
    "region": "india",
    "incident_notice_hours": 6,          # lets us meet CERT-In's 6-hour clock
    "exit_plan_rehearsed": "2026-03-10",
}

BASELINE = 0.86                          # score of the pinned snapshot on 400 cases


def summarise(complaint_text: str) -> str:
    resp = router.completion(
        model="complaints",
        messages=[{"role": "system", "content": "Summarise the complaint. Keep amounts, dates and account references."},
                  {"role": "user", "content": complaint_text}],
    )
    return resp.choices[0].message.content


def consider_new_snapshot(candidate: str) -> bool:
    """Run on a deprecation notice or a new snapshot; never switch without it."""
    score = run_eval_suite(candidate, suite="complaints_v7")     # stub: your eval harness
    if score < BASELINE - 0.02:
        alert_risk_team(f"{candidate} scored {score:.2f}; staying on {PRIMARY}")
        return False
    return True                         # propose the change through normal release review

numericDrill.question: Godavari Bank’s LLM provider offers a 99.9% monthly availability SLA. In a 30-day month, how many minutes of downtime can the provider have without breaching it?
numericDrill.answer: 30 × 24 × 60 = 43,200 minutes. 0.1% of 43,200 = 43.2 minutes. An SLA usually pays service credits, not the bank’s losses, so 43 minutes of complaint handling can stop within the SLA; a tested fallback is what keeps the service up.

interview.question: How do you run due diligence on an LLM provider for a regulated workload?
interview.answer: Start with the data terms: whether inputs are used for training, how long logs are kept, whether zero data retention is available, where processing happens and which sub-processors are involved. Read the SOC 2 Type II and ISO/IEC 27001 reports, and ISO/IEC 42001 if offered, checking that their scope covers the service you will use. Then put what matters into the contract: SLA, incident notice fast enough for your own reporting clocks, audit and regulator access, sub-processor notice, and data return and deletion on exit.

interview.question: Why pin model versions, and what does it cost you?
interview.answer: A floating alias lets the provider change the model behind the same name, so behaviour changes in production with no release on your side. Pinning a dated snapshot makes every change a deliberate upgrade that runs through your evals first. The cost is that snapshots retire, so you must track deprecation notices and budget for migrations and eval runs a few times a year.

mistakes.mistake: Treating the vendor as responsible for the vendor’s model
mistakes.fix: The regulated firm stays accountable; manage the vendor through contract, testing and monitoring

mistakes.mistake: Adding a fallback provider that has never carried traffic
mistakes.fix: Pin it, give it the same data terms, and drill the failover on a schedule

quiz.question: A bank’s complaints assistant calls ‘model-a’, a floating alias. Summaries change overnight with no release on the bank’s side. What is the most likely cause?
options: The provider moved the alias to a new model snapshot
quiz.explanation: An alias points to whichever snapshot the provider chooses. Pin a dated snapshot and upgrade only after evals.

quiz.question: A provider’s 99.9% monthly availability SLA applies to a 30-day month. How many minutes of downtime does it allow?
A payments firm sends 1,80,000 chats a month to a provider that keeps API logs for 30 days by default. Roughly how many chats sit in the provider’s logs at any time?
quiz.explanation: 30 days of logs hold about one month of traffic: about 1,80,000 chats. Zero data retention brings it to none.

quiz.question: Under SEBI’s Regulation 16C, who is responsible for the output of an AI tool a broker buys from a vendor?
options: Nobody, if the vendor is certified
quiz.explanation: The intermediary is solely responsible for the AI tools it relies on, bought or built. See the RBI and SEBI technique for the rule itself.

quiz.question: Which RBI direction sets expectations such as due diligence, audit access, concentration risk and an exit strategy when a bank outsources IT services?
options: Master Direction on Outsourcing of Information Technology Services
quiz.explanation: The 2023 Master Direction on Outsourcing of IT Services covers these for regulated entities. Educational, not legal advice.

quiz.question: An insurer’s vendor shows a SOC 2 Type II report. What should the risk team check first?
options: That the report’s scope covers the API service the insurer will use, and its period is current
Nothing: SOC 2 Type II means no risk
quiz.explanation: A report only assures the systems and period in its scope.

quiz.question: A telecom operator’s support agent runs on one provider. The provider has an 8-hour incident. With a tested fallback that switches in 15 minutes, how much outage do customers see?
quiz.explanation: A drilled fallback turns the incident into a short failover.

quiz.question: A new snapshot scores 83% on the bank’s 400-case eval suite. The pinned snapshot scores 86% and the tolerance is 2 points. What should happen?
options: Block the change and stay on the pinned snapshot

quiz.question: Which belong in an LLM provider contract for a regulated bank? Select all that apply.
options: Incident notice within a set number of hours
Audit and access rights for the bank and its regulator
A promise that the model will never make mistakes
Data return and deletion on exit
quiz.explanation: Contracts can require notice, access and exit terms; no contract can make a model error-free.

quiz.question: A hospital group wants a second LLM provider as a fallback. What makes the fallback a real control?
options: An API key in the vault
It carries traffic in regular drills, on a pinned version and with the same data terms
It is from the same provider in another region only
quiz.explanation: A fallback that has never served traffic, or has weaker data terms, fails when it is needed.

quiz.question: An NBFC’s single-provider assistant has no exit plan. Which finding is an outsourcing review most likely to raise?
options: Concentration risk and no exit strategy
quiz.explanation: Regulated entities are expected to assess concentration and plan how to exit a provider.

quiz.question: A marketplace moves two assistants to a second provider but keeps both on floating aliases. The primary alias moves 6 times a year and the fallback’s 4. How many silent behaviour changes can reach production a year?
quiz.explanation: 6 + 4 = 10. A second provider doubles the version-drift surface unless both are pinned.

quiz.question: Which are part of due diligence on an LLM provider before customer data flows? Select all that apply.
options: Whether inputs are used for training
Log retention and zero data retention options
quiz.explanation: Training use, retention and residency decide what happens to customer data.

quiz.question: A bank adds zero data retention (₹6,00,000 a year), pinned versions with evals (₹2,40,000) and a documented exit plan (₹1,20,000). What is the extra yearly cost?
Under the DPDP Act, what is a model vendor that processes customers’ personal data on a fintech’s behalf?
options: A data fiduciary with sole responsibility
A data processor, engaged under a contract, with the fintech remaining responsible
quiz.explanation: The fiduciary engages processors under a contract and stays responsible. See the DPDP technique.

quiz.question: A provider emails that a model snapshot retires in 90 days. What is the right first step?
options: Switch to the replacement the same day
Run the eval suite on the replacement and plan the migration through release review
Ignore it until the API fails
Move to a floating alias to avoid future notices
quiz.explanation: Deprecations are planned migrations: evaluate, then change through review before the date.

quiz.question: Which help manage concentration risk on a single LLM provider? Select all that apply.
options: An abstraction layer so callers do not depend on one provider’s API
Using only the provider’s newest alias
quiz.explanation: Portability, a working alternative and a known exit reduce dependence; aliases add drift, not resilience.

quiz.question: The contract requires the vendor to report security incidents to the bank within 6 hours. Why 6?
options: So the bank can meet CERT-In’s 6-hour reporting direction for cyber incidents
Because SLAs are measured in 6-hour blocks
quiz.explanation: The vendor’s notice clock must fit inside the bank’s own reporting clocks.

quiz.question: Two independent providers each have 99.9% availability. Roughly what share of the time are both down together?
quiz.explanation: 0.001 × 0.001 = 0.000001, or 0.0001%, if failures are truly independent and the fallback works.

quiz.question: A vendor quietly adds a new sub-processor in another country. Which contract clause would have given the operator a say?
options: Advance notice of new sub-processors, with a right to object
quiz.explanation: Sub-processor notice lets you check where data goes before it moves.
